sections.html:
Albemarle County surrounds Charlottesville, an independent city on the Rivanna River in central Virginia. The two are separate governments, so a city address gets its bill from the city alone. The city covers 10.27 square miles and counted 46,553 residents in 2020.

The University of Virginia shapes the housing market. Its grounds sit mostly in Albemarle County, and more than 20,000 students arrive in the academic year. Older neighborhoods close to the university, among them Ridge Street, Fifeville, Tenth and Page, and Rose Hill, hold homes with age-related repair needs that buyers spot fast. Roofs, heating systems and old windows are the items inspectors usually raise first.

Charlottesville splits real estate tax into two payments, June 5 and December 5, with any weekend deadline moving to the next Monday. The listed rate is $0.99 per $100 of assessed value, and City Council sets it each spring.

Bill detailCity of Charlottesville
Due datesJune 5 and December 5
Rate$0.99 per $100 of assessed value
Late penalty10 percent of the tax due, the day after the deadline
Interest10 percent a year, accruing monthly
Treasurer phone434-970-3146
Mailing addressP.O. Box 2854, Charlottesville, VA 22902

Penalties and interest keep running under a payment plan. Collection tools include bank account liens, rent liens and wage garnishments, and a property with three or more years of unpaid tax can be sold at a judicial sale. A penalty waiver starts with the city's Late Payment Penalty Policy and a letter to the Treasurer with supporting documents.

sections.h2: How the City Assessor values property
sections.html:
Each year the City Assessor revalues every parcel as of January 1, and change of assessment notices go out at the end of January. City code requires all real estate to be assessed annually.

The usual method is to compare recent sales of similar houses in the same neighborhood. Auctions, foreclosures, condemnations and transfers between relatives generally do not count as arm's-length sales, which helps if your own house changed hands on odd terms.

  • Assessor's office: 102 5th Street NE, Charlottesville, VA 22902, by appointment, phone 434-970-3136.
  • Mail: P.O. Box 911, Charlottesville, VA 22902.
  • Commissioner of the Revenue: 605 E Main Street, Room A-130, phone 434-970-3160.

For every parcel the Assessor maintains a history file covering owners, deed and plat references and the improvements on the lot. The city also posts assessment neighborhood maps, land books and GIS data, and its GIS Viewer opens real estate records online. A public computer at the Assessor's office offers the same access.

  • Assessment neighborhood maps and land books, found on the city's assessor pages.
  • An Income and Expense form, needed only for rental or other income-producing property.
  • The Assessment Appeal Application, available online or by calling the office.

Ahead of listing, check the record against the house itself. The city takes factual discrepancies such as square footage, acreage or the condition of improvements as grounds for appeal, and a corrected record can lower the bill the next owner inherits. If an agent files for you, include a Letter of Authorization.

Appeals climb three levels: the assessor, the Board of Equalization, then Circuit Court. Sticker shock alone does not qualify. What the city accepts is a factual error in the property record, uneven values within a neighborhood, or a dispute over fair market value.

  1. Phone the appraiser at 434-970-3136 with your owner name, address or nine-digit parcel ID. A good share of questions are settled right there.
  2. Submit an Assessment Appeal Application with your reasoning and evidence. The appraiser may inspect the property and mails a decision, which the city says arrives within 30 days.
  3. Request a Board of Equalization review within 30 days of the decision letter. Independent citizens appointed by the Circuit Court judge sit on the board, and its decision is mailed within 30 days after the hearing.
  4. Last, you can go to Circuit Court, where the proof is yours to carry and court costs are yours to pay.

The assessor's office can give you the filing deadline for the first application. Under 58.1-3379, Virginia treats the assessor's value as correct until the owner rebuts it with evidence.

Because penalty and interest are part of the Treasurer's balance, your payoff shifts from one month to the next. Call the Treasurer at 434-970-3146 for a figure tied to your closing date.

The Commissioner of the Revenue lists tax relief for older and disabled owners, a homeowner assistance program, and an exemption tied to service-connected disability for owners and surviving spouses. Ask that office which of these are open now before you count on one.

On the deed, the Virginia grantor tax in 58.1-802 comes to fifty cents on each $500 of value, and the seller normally pays it.

sections.h2: Cash sale for a Charlottesville house
sections.html:
A house that needs repairs or carries back tax can go to Cash Home Buyers for an as-is review, with the Treasurer's payoff figure built into the plan. A cash sale avoids the lender appraisal and the repair demands that often follow a financed offer, which matters most for the older homes near the university.

Before you weigh any offer, collect your latest assessment notice, tax bills and receipts, and the Treasurer's payoff figure. With those in hand you can compare offers on equal footing.

sections.h2: Timing your sale around the two installments
sections.html:
June 5 and December 5 shape the calendar. A listing in late spring or late fall tends to put an installment right at closing, so ask the Treasurer whether the current half is paid and how the year will be divided between you and the buyer.

If a payment slips while the house is under contract, the 10 percent penalty lands the next day and interest follows each month. Paying on time and sorting out the split at the settlement table costs less than waiting. The settlement agent will want a written payoff, so request one from the Treasurer's office a few days before the closing date and keep it with your receipts.

Sellers of older houses near the university also tend to face buyer inspections. Having the assessment record, the tax receipts and a clean payoff letter ready makes those negotiations simpler.

sections.h2: What to bring when you call the city
sections.html: Keep the owner name, street address and nine-digit parcel ID within reach. Three offices hold separate records, the assessor, the Treasurer and the Commissioner of the Revenue, and the same details speed up each call. Jot down who answered and what was said, particularly about penalty waivers or appeal deadlines.

faqs.q: When are Charlottesville real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Two equal installments, one on June 5 and one on December 5. Weekend deadlines roll to Monday.

faqs.q: What is the Charlottesville real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: $0.99 per $100 of assessed value is the listed rate, and City Council sets it every spring. The Treasurer can confirm the current figure.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Charlottesville assessment?
faqs.a: Phone the City Assessor at 434-970-3136 and file an Assessment Appeal Application. Unhappy with the answer? Ask the Board of Equalization for a review within 30 days. Circuit Court is the last step.

faqs.q: What happens if Charlottesville property tax goes unpaid?
faqs.a: The penalty is 10 percent and starts the day after the deadline, with interest at 10 percent yearly on top. Liens, wage garnishment and, after three or more unpaid years, a judicial sale are all possible.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Charlottesville house with tax still due?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing normally pays the balance out of your proceeds, so request a current payoff from the Treasurer's Office before the closing date.
